lead: This unit shows how to design the rotating parts that carry power from a motor to a machine. You will size shafts for strength and rigidity, choose keys and splines, select rigid or flexible couplings, and analyse clutches and brakes. After it you can take a motor rating, layout and load, and produce a safe shaft diameter, a key check and a coupling or clutch torque capacity.
about: This unit turns a rotating shaft into a safe, stiff and quiet power path. Chapter 3.1 sizes solid and hollow shafts under bending, torsion and axial load. Chapter 3.2 adds deflection limits and critical speed. Chapter 3.3 fastens the shaft to hubs with keys and splines. Chapter 3.4 joins two shafts with rigid or flexible couplings. Chapter 3.5 controls torque flow with clutches and brakes. The chain matters because a shaft is never alone: its diameter sets the key, the key sets the hub, and the coupling or clutch sets the torque that the shaft must carry. Examples use Indian workshop units: kW, rpm, N·m and MPa.

chapters.idea: A shaft must carry bending, torsion and axial load together, and its diameter is chosen from the combined stress.
chapters.depth: Start with a free-body diagram of a shaft carrying a gear or pulley. Cover solid and hollow sections. For static design use maximum shear stress theory: τ_max = 16 T_e/(π d³) for a solid shaft, where T_e is equivalent torque, T_e = √(M² + T²), M is bending moment, T is torque and d is shaft diameter. Add axial load P as a direct stress P/A, where A is cross-sectional area; then combine with bending and torsion using principal stresses. Include the ASME code idea of shock factors in torsion and bending. Some syllabi call this combined loading. Work one solid and one hollow example. Keep fatigue to Unit 2.

figure.title: Combined shaft loading
figure.aria: Block diagram showing bending, torsion and axial loads combining into stresses, principal stress and a diameter check.

chapters.example: A solid steel shaft transmits 15 kW at 900 rpm. It carries a steady bending moment of 300 N·m and an axial compressive load of 10 kN. The allowable shear stress is 40 MPa. Find the shaft diameter using the maximum shear stress theory. Take a shock factor of 1.5 on torque.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that axial load adds a direct stress; and using T_e = √(M² + T²) when P is not zero. Also mixing solid and hollow section formulas.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: direct, bending and torsional stresses; principal stresses; Unit 2: factor of safety.
chapters.leave: Fatigue factors and S-N curves to Unit 2; bearing selection to Unit 5; gear tooth loads to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A shaft that is strong enough may still be too flexible, and it must run away from its critical speed.
chapters.depth: Cover deflection and slope limits for shafts. Use double integration or Macaulay's method for stepped shafts from Unit 1. Define critical speed as the speed at which shaft whirl amplitude grows. For a simply supported shaft with a central mass, δ = W L³/(48 E I), where δ is static deflection, W is weight, L is span, E is Young's modulus and I is second moment of area; N_c = 60/(2π) √(g/δ), where N_c is critical speed in rpm and g is gravitational acceleration. Use δ in metres. Cover Rayleigh's method in words. Only a few universities teach Dunkerley's method; keep it to a short note. Distinguish critical speed from torsional resonance.

figure.aria: Plot of shaft whirl amplitude against speed ratio, with a peak at the critical speed ratio of one.

chapters.example: A steel shaft of diameter 60 mm and span 1.2 m between bearings carries a rotor of mass 25 kg at midspan. Take E = 200 GPa. Find the static deflection at midspan, the first critical speed, and state whether the deflection is below the permitted 0.08 mm.
chapters.trap: Using rpm directly in ω = √(g/δ) and mixing δ in mm with g in m/s². Critical speed is a speed, not a stress limit.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1; Unit 1: beam deflection by double integration and Macaulay's method.
chapters.leave: Multi-DOF rotor dynamics and bearing stiffness to advanced reading; vibration theory outside this unit.

chapters.idea: A key or spline is the small element that lets a shaft drive a hub without slipping.
chapters.depth: Cover sunk, saddle, round and spline joints. For a rectangular key use torque T = F d/2, where F is tangential force, d is shaft diameter and T is torque; shear check τ = F/(w L), crushing check σ_c = F/(h L/2), where w is key width, h is key height and L is key length. Define keyway stress concentration and the effect of one keyway on shaft strength. Include splines as many-key joints; only a few universities teach detailed spline stress analysis. Include key materials and fit. An added note on standard key tables completes the subject.

figure.aria: Tree of key and spline types: sunk, saddle, round, and straight or involute splines.

chapters.example: A 50 mm diameter shaft transmits 20 kW at 600 rpm through a rectangular key 14 mm wide by 9 mm high and 70 mm long. The key material has allowable shear stress 40 MPa and allowable crushing stress 80 MPa. Check the key for shear and crushing.
chapters.trap: Using full key height in crushing instead of h/2, and using T/d instead of T/(d/2) for key force.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1; Unit 1: shear stress, crushing stress and fits.
chapters.leave: Detailed spline standards and manufacturing tolerances to design handbooks; shaft strength to 3.1.

chapters.idea: A coupling passes torque from one shaft to another while allowing for small misalignment when it is flexible.
chapters.depth: Cover rigid flange and sleeve couplings, and flexible couplings: bushed pin, Oldham and universal joint. For a flange coupling, torque T = P×60/(2π N), where P is power in W and N is speed in rpm; bolt force F_b = T/(n R), where n is number of bolts and R is pitch circle radius; check bolts in shear and crushing. Include service factor. For flexible couplings, mention misalignment and torsional flexibility; do not derive rubber stiffness. Some syllabi call the flange coupling a rigid coupling. An added note on coupling alignment and balance completes the subject.

figure.aria: Tree of coupling types: rigid sleeve and flange, and flexible bushed pin, Oldham and universal couplings.

chapters.example: A rigid flange coupling connects a 30 kW, 1440 rpm motor to a machine shaft. The shaft diameter is 40 mm. Four bolts on a 120 mm pitch circle transmit the torque. The allowable shear stress in the bolts is 30 MPa and in the shaft is 40 MPa. Find the required bolt diameter and check the shaft. Use a service factor of 1.5.
chapters.trap: Applying the service factor to power but not torque, and using pitch circle diameter where radius belongs.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.3; Unit 1: fits and tolerances.
chapters.leave: Bearing loads to Unit 5; belt and chain drives to Unit 6; gearbox layout to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A clutch connects two rotating parts smoothly, and a brake does the same job by turning motion into heat.
chapters.depth: Cover single-plate and multi-plate clutches; cone and centrifugal clutches in one line, since only a few universities teach their details. For uniform wear, T = μ W (r_o + r_i)/2, where μ is coefficient of friction, W is axial force, r_o is outer radius and r_i is inner radius. For uniform pressure, T = (2/3) μ W (r_o³ - r_i³)/(r_o² - r_i²). Multiply by the number of friction surfaces. Brake torque uses the same friction formula; heat generated is E = T Δω t, where Δω is relative angular speed and t is slip time. Include block brake and shoe brake sketches. Keep thermal stress analysis out.

figure.title: Clutch and brake in a drivetrain
figure.aria: Block diagram of a drivetrain: engine torque passes through clutch and gearbox to the wheel; the brake turns wheel motion into heat.

chapters.example: A single-plate clutch has outer radius 150 mm and inner radius 100 mm. The coefficient of friction is 0.3 and the axial force is 5 kN. Find the torque capacity using uniform wear theory. If the engine runs at 1200 rpm, find the power transmitted. Estimate the heat generated per engagement if the clutch slips for 0.5 s at a relative speed of 600 rpm.
chapters.trap: Using the uniform pressure formula for a worn-in clutch, and forgetting to multiply by the number of friction surfaces.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1; Unit 1: friction and power; Chapter 3.4 for torque flow.
chapters.leave: Brake lining thermal stress and detailed cone or centrifugal clutch design to advanced notes; bearing and gearbox details to Units 5 and 7.
